content.title: About
content.content: Acorn squash (Cucurbita pepo) is a small winter squash with a ridged, dark green (sometimes orange-streaked) rind, shaped like an acorn, with mildly sweet, nutty, yellow-orange flesh. It originated in the Americas and is usually baked or roasted in halves and stuffed. Acorn squash keeps well for weeks to months after harvest.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Acorn squash is named for its acorn-like shape.
It is a winter squash, harvested when mature and with a hard rind.
Its skin is edible when roasted, which makes preparation easy.
It is botanically the same species as zucchini and many pumpkins.
It is often served in halves, stuffed with grains, vegetables, or meat.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Acorn squash contributes fiber that supports digestion and fullness.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Provides potassium, magnesium, and manganese
items.content: These minerals support normal blood pressure, muscle function, and metabolism.

items.title: Contains carotenoids and B vitamins
items.content: Acorn squash provides carotenoids that the body can convert into vitamin A, and some B vitamins.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Acorn squash is relatively low in calories for its volume.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Squash allergy is uncommon but can occur.

items.title: Natural sugar content
items.content: Acorn squash contains natural sugars and starch, so portions matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Potassium considerations
items.content: People with kidney problems or on certain medications should consult a healthcare professional about potassium intake.

items.title: Bitter squash
items.content: Rarely, squash can contain high levels of bitter cucurbitacins that can cause stomach upset. Discard squash that tastes very bitter.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Acorn squash can be halved, seeded, and baked or roasted cut-side down, then filled with grains, vegetables, nuts, or sausage, or drizzled with butter, olive oil, or maple syrup. It can also be steamed, microwaved, or pureed into soups. The skin is edible when roasted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole acorn squash in a cool, dry, well-ventilated place for several weeks to a couple of months. Cut squash should be wrapped and refrigerated and used within about five days. Cooked squash can be refrigerated for three to five days or frozen.
